description: God Eye Researcher 深度研究代理的評測題庫，涵蓋台灣製造、金融、零售、科技與政策領域企業客戶常見的中英文研究問題，並以可明確判定是否達成的評分準則檢核報告品質。

questions.question: 台灣電子製造業（PCB、SMT組裝、半導體封測）導入AI視覺檢測（AI瑕疵檢測）的現況如何？主要導入模式、實際效益與常見失敗原因有哪些？
questions.audience: 製造業客戶的廠長與數位轉型主管

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary answer about the current state of AI visual inspection adoption in Taiwanese electronics manufacturing within the first paragraph.
Distinguishes deep-learning-based inspection from conventional rule-based AOI and explains what AI adds (e.g., reducing false calls / overkill).
Addresses at least two of the named sub-sectors (PCB, SMT assembly, semiconductor packaging and testing) separately rather than treating electronics as one undifferentiated segment.
Describes deployment patterns, such as adding AI re-judgment to existing AOI machines versus new integrated systems, and edge versus cloud inference.

Every quantitative benefit claim (e.g., false-call reduction, labor savings, yield gain) is attributed to a named company or source and states its scope or date, rather than presented as a generic industry figure.
Discusses common failure causes such as scarce defect samples or class imbalance, inconsistent labeling, model drift after product changeovers, or difficulty integrating with MES.
Cites at least one Taiwanese institutional source (e.g., ITRI, III/MIC, or a government ministry) and at least one company case study or vendor-independent source.
Explains why reported benefits vary widely between cases (e.g., baseline AOI false-call rate, product mix, defect types) instead of only listing figures.
Names at least two concrete Taiwanese manufacturers or local solution providers with documented deployments, each linked to a source.
States which reported results are vendor or self-reported claims that could not be independently verified.

questions.notes: Core customer scenario for the user's manufacturing accounts; tests whether the agent uses Traditional Chinese local sources, separates sub-sectors, and avoids repeating vendor marketing numbers as fact.

questions.question: 台灣工具機與精密機械產業在預測性維護上有哪些實際落地案例？通常使用哪些感測資料與模型方法？中小型工廠導入的門檻與成本結構大概如何？
questions.audience: 工具機廠研發主管與工廠IT/OT負責人

rubric.criterion: Describes the main sensor data types used for machine-tool predictive maintenance (e.g., vibration, spindle current or load, temperature, acoustic emission) and which failure modes each helps detect.
Compares modeling approaches such as threshold or rule-based monitoring, anomaly detection, and remaining-useful-life (RUL) prediction, including when each is appropriate.
Presents at least two concrete cases from Taiwanese machine-tool makers, component makers, or their customers, each with a cited source.
Addresses data acquisition from CNC controllers (e.g., via OPC UA, MTConnect, or controller-vendor interfaces) and the challenge of heterogeneous legacy machines.
Discusses barriers specific to small and medium-sized factories, such as upfront sensor or retrofit cost, lack of data-science staff, and scarcity of recorded failure events.
Any cost or ROI figure is given with currency, scope (per machine, per line, or per plant) and source date, or the report explicitly says such figures are not publicly available.
Cites at least one Taiwanese government or research-institute source (e.g., ITRI, the Precision Machinery Research & Development Center, or a Ministry of Economic Affairs program).
Explains why many predictive-maintenance pilots fail to scale (e.g., too few labeled failures, no integration into maintenance workflows) rather than only listing success stories.
Acknowledges where case-study results are self-reported or lack a before/after baseline.
Ends with a phased adoption path or decision checklist suited to a small or medium-sized manufacturer.

questions.notes: Taichung precision-machinery cluster is a frequent SME customer segment; tests practical depth (protocols, legacy retrofit) and honesty about thin public cost data.

questions.question: 歐盟CBAM（碳邊境調整機制）正式上路後，對台灣螺絲螺帽與鋼鐵製品出口商的實際影響是什麼？我們需要準備哪些排放資料與查證？台灣的碳費能不能拿來抵減？
questions.audience: 出口製造業的永續長與財務長

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer summarizing the expected impact on Taiwanese fastener and steel-product exporters in the first paragraph.
Distinguishes CBAM's transitional reporting period from its definitive period and gives the start date of each.
Explains product scope by reference to CN codes or product categories and explicitly addresses whether fasteners fall within scope.
Explains that the legal obligation sits with the EU importer or authorised CBAM declarant, and what is expected from the non-EU producer (supplying embedded-emissions data).
Describes the emissions data required, including direct and indirect emissions, and the role of default values versus actual installation-level data.
Addresses verification requirements for emissions data in the definitive period, including who may act as a verifier.
Explains how a carbon price paid in the country of origin can be deducted under CBAM and evaluates whether Taiwan's carbon fee under the Climate Change Response Act would qualify.
States the status and date of any CBAM simplification or amendment it mentions (e.g., de minimis thresholds), distinguishing adopted changes from proposals.
Considers upstream supply-chain implications, such as reliance on steel wire-rod suppliers for emissions data and the difference between blast-furnace and electric-arc-furnace steel.

Cites primary EU sources (the CBAM Regulation text or European Commission guidance) for EU claims and at least one official Taiwanese source (e.g., Ministry of Environment or Ministry of Economic Affairs) for Taiwan claims.
Illustrates cost exposure with a worked example whose assumptions (e.g., emission intensity, EU ETS price, free-allocation phase-out) are stated explicitly.
States which elements remain uncertain, such as pending implementing acts, future carbon prices, or whether Taiwan's carbon fee will be recognized.

questions.notes: Fasteners are a major Taiwanese export to the EU; the question requires combining EU primary law, Taiwan's domestic carbon pricing and supply-chain reasoning, and has moving parts that test date discipline.

questions.question: Where is generative AI actually being used in semiconductor manufacturing today (yield analysis, defect classification, equipment maintenance, engineering knowledge assistants)? Separate production deployments from pilots and vendor demos, and explain what architectures fabs use given their IP-confidentiality constraints.
questions.audience: Solutions architects and manufacturing-industry account teams

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary stating which use cases have evidence of production deployment versus pilot only.

Covers at least four distinct use-case areas, such as yield or root-cause analysis, defect classification, predictive equipment maintenance, recipe or process optimization, and engineering knowledge assistants.
Labels each cited example with its maturity status (production, pilot, research, or vendor demo) and the date of the source.
Distinguishes generative AI / LLM approaches from conventional machine learning already established in fabs (e.g., automatic defect classification, virtual metrology) rather than conflating them.
Describes architectures used to protect process IP, such as on-premises or air-gapped deployment, privately hosted models, or retrieval over internal documents without data leaving the fab.
Addresses offerings from semiconductor equipment, EDA, or yield-analytics vendors in addition to fab-built solutions.
Backs company-specific claims with primary sources such as company press releases, earnings-call remarks, technical conference papers, or official engineering blogs, not only secondary news.
Cites at least one peer-reviewed paper or technical conference publication (e.g., from an IEEE or SPIE venue) for a technical claim.
Explains why LLM adoption is slower or harder in fabs than in other industries (e.g., data confidentiality, need for deterministic results, low tolerance for hallucination in process decisions).
Discusses how LLM outputs are validated or kept human-in-the-loop for engineering decisions.
Identifies which use cases are most transferable to a Taiwanese fab or OSAT customer and explains why.
States that many fab deployments are undisclosed and that the available evidence is therefore incomplete or biased toward publicized cases.

questions.notes: High hype-to-evidence ratio; a good report must grade maturity per example and resist treating announcements as deployments. Directly relevant to Taiwan semiconductor accounts.

questions.question: For a multi-plant manufacturer modernizing its industrial data architecture, how does a Unified Namespace built on MQTT/Sparkplug B compare with an OPC UA-centric or ISA-95 layered approach? When does each make sense and what are the main pitfalls?
questions.audience: OT/IT architects at a manufacturing customer

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct decision framework stating when each approach fits, in the first paragraph or summary.
Explains what a Unified Namespace is and makes clear it is an architectural pattern rather than a product or formal standard.
Explains the roles of MQTT, Sparkplug B, and OPC UA (including OPC UA PubSub) and how they can be combined rather than treated as mutually exclusive.
Relates the approaches to ISA-95 levels or the traditional automation pyramid.
Addresses OT security considerations, such as broker hardening, network segmentation, or alignment with IEC 62443.
Discusses operational pitfalls, such as topic or namespace governance, consistent data modeling across plants, and broker scalability or high availability.
Cites standards-body or specification sources (e.g., OPC Foundation, Eclipse Foundation for Sparkplug, OASIS for MQTT, or ISA) for protocol claims.
Explains why practitioner opinions on UNS diverge (e.g., community and vendor advocacy versus established OPC UA ecosystems) instead of presenting one view as consensus.
Explains how the plant data layer connects to cloud analytics or a data lake, including edge-gateway considerations.
Notes where claims rely on practitioner blogs or vendor content rather than independent evaluations.

questions.notes: Architecture-comparison question where much of the web content is opinionated; tests balance, standards-level sourcing and whether the agent recognizes UNS is a pattern, not a standard.

questions.question: Which parts of IEC 62443 apply to us as a factory operator versus our machine suppliers and system integrators, and what is a realistic first step toward compliance?
questions.audience: Plant IT/OT security managers

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer mapping roles to IEC 62443 parts in the first paragraph.
Distinguishes the three principal roles: asset owner, system integrator or service provider, and product supplier.
Maps each role to specific numbered parts of the series (e.g., 4-1 and 4-2 for product suppliers) rather than referring to the standard only as a whole.
Explains the concepts of zones, conduits, and security levels.
Proposes a concrete first step for the factory operator, such as an asset inventory and risk assessment, and explains why it comes first.
Cites ISA, IEC, the ISA Global Cybersecurity Alliance, or a government cybersecurity agency rather than only vendor blogs.
Explains how certification differs by role (product certification versus process or capability certification) and what an operator can reasonably require from suppliers in procurement.
Notes that the standard texts are paywalled and that the report relies on summaries, or otherwise states the limits of its access to primary text.

questions.notes: Quick, well-scoped standards question; checks role mapping precision and whether the agent admits it could not read the paywalled primary text.

questions.question: 台灣的銀行、保險與證券業者若要把核心系統或客戶資料放上公有雲，金管會對資料存放地點、委外申請與稽核權有哪些具體規範？跟新加坡MAS、香港HKMA的做法相比有什麼差異？
questions.audience: 金融業資訊長、法遵與風險管理主管

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer summarizing whether, and under what conditions, Taiwanese financial institutions may store customer data offshore in a public cloud.
Identifies the main Taiwanese regulation governing outsourcing including cloud services (金融機構作業委託他人處理內部作業制度及程序辦法) and states when it was last amended.
Explains the rules on data location, including the conditions for storing customer data outside Taiwan and any requirement for domestic backup or regulator approval.
Explains whether and how approval or notification requirements differ depending on the materiality of the outsourced activity.
Addresses the audit and access rights the financial institution and the FSC must retain over the cloud service provider, including on-site inspection rights.
Covers differences across banking, insurance, and securities, or states that the same rules apply to all three and notes any sector-specific guidance.
Addresses industry self-regulatory guidance issued by the relevant trade associations (e.g., the Bankers Association), or states that none was found.
Compares Taiwan with Singapore MAS and Hong Kong HKMA requirements on at least data location, regulator access, and approval or notification.
Every cited regulation or guideline is given with its official name and the date or year of the version relied upon.
Cites the official regulation text (e.g., the Laws & Regulations Database of the R.O.C. or the FSC website) rather than only law-firm or vendor summaries for Taiwan claims.
Links specific regulatory requirements to concrete architecture choices (e.g., use of an in-country cloud region, customer-managed encryption keys, or a hybrid design).
Distinguishes binding regulations from guidance, FAQs, and supervisory practice, and states where actual approval practice could not be verified from public sources.

questions.notes: Data-residency question that FSI customers ask in nearly every engagement; requires primary Taiwanese legal text plus cross-jurisdiction comparison, and tests separation of law from practice.

questions.question: 台灣銀行業目前導入生成式AI的主要應用場景有哪些？金管會的金融業AI指引對這些應用提出了哪些治理要求？
questions.audience: 銀行數位金融與法遵部門主管

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer listing the main generative AI use cases and the core governance expectations in the first paragraph.
Identifies the Taiwan FSC's AI guidance for the financial sector (core principles and/or guidelines) by official name and publication date.
Summarizes the governance requirements in the FSC guidance, such as risk-based assessment, accountability, fairness, privacy protection, transparency or explainability, and third-party management.

Describes at least four concrete use cases (e.g., customer-service chatbots, internal knowledge search, document processing, coding assistance, marketing content), with at least two attributed to named Taiwanese financial institutions.
Labels each named bank case with its stage (announced, pilot, or production) and the date of the source.
Explains how the guidance treats outsourced or third-party AI models, including foundation models hosted by foreign cloud providers.
Cites the FSC's own publication or press release for the guidance and primary bank announcements for the case examples.
Explains which use cases are lower-risk under the guidance (internal, human-reviewed) versus higher-risk (customer-facing, credit decisions) and why adoption has concentrated in the former.
States whether the guidance is legally binding or advisory and how it relates to existing rules such as the Personal Data Protection Act and outsourcing regulations.
States which aspects of banks' actual practices could not be verified from public sources.

questions.notes: Combines regulator text with case evidence; tests whether the agent ties use cases to governance expectations instead of producing two disconnected lists.

questions.question: 台灣開放銀行目前推動到哪個階段？各階段開放哪些資料或服務，第三方業者又是怎麼參與的？
questions.audience: 銀行數位金融部門與金融科技合作夥伴

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer stating the current phase of Taiwan's open banking with an as-of date.
Describes each of the three phases (public product information, customer account information, and transaction-related services) and what data or services each covers.
Explains Taiwan's market-led rather than mandated approach and identifies the roles of the regulator, the industry association, and the API platform operator.
Describes how third-party service providers participate, including partnership or onboarding requirements and customer consent.
Gives the launch or announcement date for each phase that has started.
Cites at least one official FSC, Bankers Association, or API platform operator source.
Explains why uptake in Taiwan has differed from mandated regimes such as the UK or Australia, rather than only describing the phases.
States what could not be confirmed, such as the number of participating banks and third-party providers or the exact status of the latest phase.

questions.notes: Short factual status question with a stable structure; checks as-of dating and that the agent explains Taiwan's self-regulatory model.

questions.question: How are banks in Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong using machine learning and generative AI for scam/fraud detection and AML transaction monitoring, and what results and regulatory expectations have been published?
questions.audience: Financial-services solutions architects and bank risk-technology leads

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary of the main approaches in use and the strength of evidence for their results.
Distinguishes fraud/scam detection from AML transaction monitoring and explains how their data, latency requirements, and regulatory obligations differ.
Covers all three jurisdictions named in the question with at least one concrete initiative or case each.
Describes regulator- or industry-led information-sharing platforms (e.g., MAS COSMIC in Singapore, or HKMA-supported initiatives) and their relevance to ML models.
Addresses Taiwan's anti-fraud legal framework (e.g., the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act) and what it requires of banks regarding suspicious-account detection.

Describes the ML techniques in use (e.g., supervised classifiers, graph analytics for mule networks, anomaly detection) and where generative AI is used (e.g., alert triage, investigation narrative drafting).
Every performance claim (e.g., false-positive reduction) is attributed to a named institution or vendor with the date and scope of the measurement.
Cites at least one regulator or standard-setter source (e.g., MAS, HKMA, Taiwan FSC, or FATF) for regulatory expectations.
Explains the trade-off between false-positive reduction and the explainability/auditability regulators expect, rather than treating accuracy gains as unambiguous.
States that many performance figures are vendor-reported and identifies which could not be independently verified.

questions.notes: Scam prevention is a top priority for Taiwanese banks; the question forces multi-jurisdiction synthesis and separation of fraud vs AML, which weaker reports conflate.

questions.question: Does the EU's DORA apply to a Taiwanese bank with a branch or subsidiary in the EU, and what does it require from our cloud providers?
questions.audience: Compliance and IT risk managers at a Taiwanese bank

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct yes / no / it-depends answer and names the conditions it depends on.
Distinguishes an EU-incorporated subsidiary from an EU branch of a non-EU bank when assessing applicability, and explains the basis for each conclusion.
States DORA's full name or regulation number and its date of application.
Summarizes what DORA requires of ICT third-party service arrangements (e.g., mandatory contractual provisions, exit strategies, register of information).
Explains the oversight framework for critical ICT third-party providers and that designation is made by the European Supervisory Authorities.
Cites the regulation text on EUR-Lex or official EBA, EIOPA, or ESMA materials.
Explains how DORA obligations interact with the Taiwanese parent's FSC outsourcing obligations (e.g., overlaps or potential conflicts in audit rights or data location).
Flags where the answer depends on legal interpretation or national competent authority practice and recommends confirmation with counsel or the regulator.

questions.notes: Quick applicability question with a genuine legal nuance (branch vs subsidiary); tests hedging and cross-regime insight rather than a generic DORA summary.

questions.question: 台灣連鎖零售（便利商店、超市、量販店）做需求預測時，傳統統計模型、機器學習（例如梯度提升樹）和時間序列基礎模型（例如Chronos、TimesFM）各有什麼優缺點？生鮮和短效期商品應該怎麼選？
questions.audience: 零售業供應鏈規劃與資料科學團隊

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct recommendation on which approach suits which product or data situation.
Compares all three approach families named in the question on accuracy, data requirements, and operational cost.
Addresses challenges specific to fresh and short-shelf-life products, such as intermittent demand, the asymmetry between waste and stockout costs, and promotion effects.
Discusses hierarchical forecasting across store, SKU, and time levels and the need for reconciliation.
Cites empirical benchmark evidence such as the M5 forecasting competition or peer-reviewed evaluations, not only vendor claims.
Every accuracy comparison names the metric used (e.g., WAPE, MASE, WRMSSE) and the dataset or benchmark it was measured on.
Addresses external drivers relevant to Taiwan retail, such as weather and typhoons, holidays like Lunar New Year, and promotional calendars.
Explains the conditions under which each approach wins (e.g., foundation models with sparse history versus tuned gradient boosting with rich covariates) rather than declaring a universal winner.
States the current availability status of any managed AWS forecasting service it recommends (e.g., whether it is closed to new customers) and offers an alternative path where needed.
States that public evidence specific to Taiwanese retailers is limited and identifies which conclusions are extrapolated from other markets.

questions.notes: Method-comparison question with a fast-moving component (time-series foundation models); tests benchmark literacy, metric precision, and awareness of AWS service lifecycle changes.

questions.question: 台灣電商平台和零售品牌用生成式AI做商品文案和智慧客服，有哪些公開的實際案例和成效？
questions.audience: 電商平台營運主管

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary of the main use cases and the overall strength of evidence on outcomes.
Presents at least three concrete cases involving Taiwanese e-commerce platforms or retail brands, each with a cited source.
Covers both product-content generation and customer-service use cases rather than only one.
Every reported outcome metric (e.g., conversion, handling time, resolution rate) is attributed to its source with a date and scope.
Addresses Traditional Chinese output quality and Taiwan-specific terminology as a practical concern.
Uses primary sources such as company announcements or official case studies for each case, not only aggregator articles.
Explains why reported metrics are hard to attribute to generative AI alone or hard to compare across companies.
States which cases lacked outcome data or could not be verified beyond the company's own claims.

questions.notes: Quick case-scan in Traditional Chinese sources; tests whether the agent finds real local cases and flags thin outcome evidence instead of padding.

questions.question: How are retailers in Asia-Pacific building retail media networks, and what data clean room and privacy-preserving technologies are they using to share first-party data with brands?
questions.audience: Retail industry account teams and data architects

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary of the main retail media network models and the role clean rooms play.
Defines a retail media network and distinguishes on-site, off-site, and in-store media.
Presents at least three Asia-Pacific retailer examples (e.g., from Taiwan, Japan, Singapore, Australia, or Southeast Asia) with cited sources.
Explains how data clean rooms work and compares at least two approaches or vendors (e.g., cloud-provider clean rooms versus specialist vendors).
Addresses legal constraints on sharing loyalty-program data with reference to at least one Asia-Pacific privacy law, such as Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act.
Discusses measurement and attribution challenges, such as closed-loop measurement, incrementality testing, and the lack of common standards.
Cites at least one industry-standards body or regulator source (e.g., IAB measurement guidelines or a data protection authority) in addition to vendor or retailer sources.
Every market-size figure is given with currency, year, geographic scope, and the name of the research firm.
Explains why Asia-Pacific retail media maturity differs from the US (e.g., market fragmentation, marketplace or super-app dominance, differing privacy regimes).
Notes that market-size estimates and definitions differ across research firms and states which figures could not be reconciled.

questions.notes: Blends business strategy with data architecture and privacy; market-size numbers vary wildly across sources, so this tests number hygiene and reconciliation.

questions.question: What independent evidence is there that AI computer-vision loss prevention (self-checkout monitoring, shelf cameras, shrink analytics) actually reduces retail shrink, how does the cost compare with the benefit, and what privacy and legal risks would a grocery chain in Taiwan or Japan face in deploying it?
questions.audience: Retail executives evaluating a loss-prevention investment

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer on the strength of evidence for shrink reduction in the first paragraph.
Distinguishes the main solution types (self-checkout non-scan detection, shelf or sweep monitoring, POS exception analytics, facial recognition) and evaluates the evidence for each separately.
Separates vendor-reported results from independent evaluations and cites at least one independent source (e.g., academic research or an industry body such as ECR Retail Loss).
Defines shrink and states which components (external theft, internal theft, process error, damage) each cited figure covers.
Discusses how self-checkout itself affects loss rates, as context for why computer-vision monitoring is deployed.
Provides a cost-benefit framing with explicit assumptions (e.g., store revenue, baseline shrink rate, hardware and subscription costs) rather than an unqualified ROI claim.
Addresses customer-experience side effects, such as false accusations, checkout friction, or added staff intervention.
Analyzes privacy constraints under Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act, including how video and any biometric data are classified and what notice or consent is needed.
Analyzes the same issues under Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information, including any regulator guidance on camera-based facial recognition for crime prevention.
Explains why reported shrink-reduction results vary widely (e.g., baseline shrink, store format, deterrence versus detection effects, measurement period) instead of averaging them.
Identifies lower-risk deployment options (e.g., non-biometric object detection, on-device processing, short retention) that keep most of the benefit with less legal exposure.
States what could not be verified, such as effects beyond pilot periods or results specific to Taiwan or Japan.

questions.notes: Evidence-quality question in a vendor-dominated space plus a two-jurisdiction privacy analysis; strong reports grade evidence and give a conditional cost model.

questions.question: 企業要做繁體中文（台灣用語）的生成式AI應用，目前有哪些模型和評測基準可以參考？國際大型模型和台灣在地模型（例如TAIDE、Breeze）實際表現差多少？
questions.audience: 企業AI團隊與解決方案架構師

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer summarizing how international and Taiwan-local models compare for Traditional Chinese enterprise use.
Identifies at least two Traditional Chinese or Taiwan-specific evaluation benchmarks (e.g., TMMLU+) and describes what each measures.
Covers both international frontier or open-weight models and Taiwan-local or locally fine-tuned models (e.g., TAIDE, MediaTek Research Breeze).
Every cited benchmark score states the model version, benchmark version, evaluation setting (e.g., zero-shot or few-shot), and date.
Addresses Taiwan-specific language issues beyond benchmarks, such as Simplified Chinese leakage, mainland versus Taiwan terminology, and cultural or political framing.
Discusses licensing and deployment considerations for local models, such as commercial-use license terms, on-premises hosting, and model size versus inference cost.
Cites primary sources such as model cards, technical reports, or benchmark papers rather than only news articles.
Explains why benchmark rankings may not predict performance on a specific enterprise task and recommends building a task-specific evaluation set.
Explains the trade-off between a larger general-purpose model and a smaller locally tuned model in terms of quality, cost, and data sovereignty.
States the as-of date of the comparison, notes that model releases change quickly, and lists any results it could not verify.

questions.notes: Recurring question from Taiwanese enterprises; tests local-source discovery, benchmark-reporting precision, and recognition of terminology/framing issues that generic reports miss.

questions.question: Compare managed vector database options for a production RAG system on AWS (OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector, Amazon S3 Vectors, and third-party services such as Pinecone or MongoDB Atlas) on cost, scale, latency, filtering, and operational burden.
questions.audience: Solutions architects designing RAG workloads

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct recommendation summary mapping workload profiles (e.g., corpus size, latency target, query volume) to options.
Compares every option named in the question on each of the five named dimensions: cost, scale, latency, filtering, and operational burden.
Explains the indexing algorithms involved (e.g., HNSW, IVF) and how they affect recall, memory footprint, and build time.
Addresses hybrid (keyword plus vector) search support and metadata filtering behavior, including pre-filtering versus post-filtering.
States pricing models with units and as-of dates (e.g., per compute-unit hour, per GB stored, per million queries) rather than vague cost statements.
States the preview or general-availability status of each service or key feature with a date.
Cites official AWS and vendor documentation or pricing pages for capability and price claims.
Explains why published vendor benchmarks are hard to compare (e.g., different datasets, recall targets, hardware) instead of quoting them as directly comparable.
Addresses integration with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases or other managed RAG tooling, including which vector stores are supported.
States which comparisons could not be verified with independent benchmarks and proposes a proof-of-concept test plan.

questions.notes: Classic SA comparison with fast-changing pricing and feature status; tests documentation-grounded claims, dated pricing, and benchmark skepticism.

questions.question: What are current best practices for evaluating enterprise RAG and agentic systems before and after production launch, covering metrics, open-source frameworks, LLM-as-judge reliability, and human review?
questions.audience: ML engineers and solutions architects

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary of a recommended evaluation approach.
Separates retrieval metrics (e.g., context precision/recall, hit rate, MRR) from generation metrics (e.g., faithfulness or groundedness, answer relevance).
Addresses evaluation of agentic systems specifically, such as tool-call correctness, trajectory or multi-step task success, and cost and latency per task.
Compares at least three evaluation frameworks or services (e.g., RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens, managed cloud evaluation services) with their scope and limitations.
Discusses known reliability issues of LLM-as-judge (e.g., position bias, verbosity bias, self-preference) and mitigations such as calibration against human labels.
Cites at least one peer-reviewed or arXiv research paper on LLM-as-judge reliability or RAG evaluation.
Covers online production evaluation, such as user feedback signals, tracing, sampling for human review, and regression testing against a golden dataset.
Explains why offline benchmark scores often fail to predict production quality and how to build a representative test set.
Addresses evaluating non-English or multilingual output (e.g., Traditional Chinese), including judge-model language bias.
Acknowledges the lack of standardized metrics and states which recommendations rest on practitioner consensus rather than controlled studies.

questions.notes: Self-referential for this project (rubric-based evaluation); tests mixing research literature with practitioner tooling and honesty about an immature field.

questions.question: 台灣企業導入生成式AI時，在個資法、著作權法，以及人工智慧基本法等AI相關法規上，目前要注意哪些合規重點？
questions.audience: 企業法務長與資安長

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct summary of the key compliance obligations in the first paragraph.
States the legislative status of Taiwan's AI Basic Act (人工智慧基本法) with a date, clearly distinguishing enacted law from draft or proposed provisions.
Explains how Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act applies to personal data used in prompts, fine-tuning, or RAG knowledge bases, including purpose limitation and cross-border transfer.
Addresses the status of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Commission and the most recent Personal Data Protection Act amendments, with dates.
Addresses copyright on both the input side (using copyrighted material for training or retrieval) and the output side (copyrightability of AI-generated content and infringement risk).
Cites official Taiwanese sources, such as the Laws & Regulations Database, the Executive Yuan, the Ministry of Digital Affairs, or the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office, for legal claims.
Covers sector-specific guidance that may apply on top of general law (e.g., FSC guidance for financial institutions or Executive Yuan guidance on public-sector generative AI use).
Translates legal requirements into concrete internal controls (e.g., data classification, prompt logging, vendor contract terms, human review) rather than only restating the law.
Identifies areas where Taiwanese law is unsettled or untested in court and explains the practical risk this creates.
States that the report is not legal advice and identifies which points require confirmation with counsel because of pending legislation or lack of precedent.

questions.notes: Tests legislative-status discipline in a moving area and whether the agent turns law into controls; requires official Taiwanese legal sources.

questions.question: We are a Taiwanese manufacturer exporting industrial machinery and robots to the EU, and our products include AI-based vision and safety functions. What are our obligations under the EU AI Act, when do they apply, and how does the Act interact with the new EU Machinery Regulation and CE marking?
questions.audience: Executive management and compliance leads at a Taiwanese exporter

rubric.criterion: Opens with a direct answer summarizing the likely risk classification and the main obligations.

Explains the high-risk route for AI that is a safety component of a product covered by EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (such as machinery), and contrasts it with the use-case-based high-risk categories in Annex III.
Identifies the company's likely role as provider and explains the obligations of other supply-chain actors (importer, distributor, deployer).
Explains the requirement for non-EU providers to appoint an authorised representative established in the EU.

Summarizes provider obligations for high-risk AI systems, including risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, quality management, and conformity assessment.
States the AI Act's entry-into-force date and the application dates for obligations relevant to this company, distinguishing Annex I from Annex III high-risk systems.
Reports any proposed changes or postponements to the AI Act timeline with their legislative status and date, without presenting proposals as adopted law.

Explains how the AI Act interacts with the EU Machinery Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1230), including that regulation's application date and the roles of conformity assessment, notified bodies, and CE marking.
Addresses the role and development status of harmonised standards for the AI Act (e.g., work by CEN-CENELEC JTC 21).
Cites the official regulation text on EUR-Lex and at least one European Commission or AI Office publication.
Provides a prioritized action plan separating what to do now from what can wait until closer to application dates, linked to specific obligations.
States which points depend on pending guidelines, standards, or legal interpretation and could not be resolved from public sources.

questions.notes: Realistic exporter scenario requiring two interacting EU regimes, role analysis, and careful date handling amid proposed timeline changes; a strong test of deep regulatory synthesis.
